units: the training space is made up of four separate stations
the first station is for sorting and washing the raw material
marking out calls for careful checking so that faults do not appear at assembly
the assembly stage uses clamping tools worked by two people
the last station brings together sanding, finishing and the checking of dimensions
a sheet on display gives the order of operations, the tolerances allowed and the safety equipment
the instructor moves about to correct how the learners handle their tools
all the stations must have been passed through before anyone may work unsupervised
text: A training workshop for handwork is laid out as four separate stations, and each one covers its own family of movements. At the first, the raw material is sorted: the learner weighs it, grades it and washes off whatever would spoil the later steps. The second deals with marking out, where careful checking of the reference points keeps faults from turning up at assembly. Assembly follows, with vices, clamps and a screw press that two learners work between them. The last station, often thought the dullest, brings together sanding, finishing and the checking of dimensions. A sheet pinned to the wall gives the order of operations, the tolerances allowed and the protective clothing required. The instructor moves about, adjusting a grip here, straightening a posture there. Nobody is cleared to work unsupervised until all four stations have been passed through.

units: passing on a craft was at first done by watching and repeating beside an older worker
the coming of writing set the procedures down in books
moving pictures then promised a clearer explanation
the writer disputes the idea that this sequence is steady progress
each support gains in reach what it loses in human presence
a written work reaches distant readers but corrects no movement
a recording shows the movement from every angle without feeling the hesitation of the person watching
the conclusion put forward is that no support replaces the presence of an older worker
text: For a long stretch of time, a craft passed from hand to hand: the learner watched an older worker, copied, failed and began again. Writing changed that. Once the procedures were set down in books they held still, open to anyone able to read them. Moving pictures came later and promised a clearer explanation, with the diagram that unfolds and the step slowed right down. I do not accept that this sequence amounts to steady progress. Every support has gained in reach exactly what it has lost in presence. A written work finds readers no workshop would ever have taken in, yet it cannot correct a hand that shakes. A recording shows the movement from every angle and feels nothing of the hesitation in the person watching. My conclusion is short: no support replaces an older worker leaning over an unfinished piece.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: an injury to the hand marked the start of her path
she had to work out unusual grips to hold her tools
that constraint made her alert to the way each person handles an instrument
she gained a name as a very fine teacher
she breaks every movement into stages for beginners
her workshop took in learners who had been turned away elsewhere
she cut back her own output in order to teach more
that choice brought her earnings down
her former learners, now experts, still use her method
text: The bookbinder in question lost the use of two fingers when she was young, and that injury shaped the path she took. Unable to hold the folder as her fellows did, she had to work out grips nobody had shown her, which left her unusually alert to the way each person takes hold of a tool. That alertness earned her, years later, a name as a very fine teacher. Because she had broken every movement into stages to make it possible for herself, she could do the same with the movements of an awkward beginner. Her workshop began to draw learners other workshops had turned away. As demand rose she cut back her own output and gave her afternoons over to teaching. Her earnings fell because of it, though the method spread: her former learners, seasoned now, still take a movement apart the way she taught them.

units: the beginner's handbook is irritating from the opening pages
the author piles up definitions and breaks off proofs with asides
the reader finishes a chapter without knowing what has been taken from it
the material itself is judged to be good
the criticism bears on the arrangement and not on the subject matter
reading it the other way round, starting with the exercises, solved the problem
the exercises are graded and honest about how hard they are
the book then becomes a store where one looks for what is missing
the advice is to open the theory only at the point where one gets stuck
text: Honestly, this beginner's handbook irritated me from the opening pages. The writing is dense: the author piles up definitions, doubles back, drops an aside in the middle of a proof. You finish a chapter with no idea what you were meant to take from it. The maddening part is that the material is good, and only the arrangement lets it down. So I tried something odd and read the thing the other way round, starting with the exercises. That sorted it out. The exercises are graded and honest about how hard each one is. Work through them first and you learn what you are short of, then go hunting for the definition you lack. The book turns into a store you dip into rather than a corridor you are marched along. I do recommend it, then, with one instruction: begin at the end, and open the theory only where you get stuck.

units: the writer reports on two courses taken in the same term
the first brought a large group together in a tiered room
the speaker there talked without being interrupted
the second gathered a very small number round a table
the woman leading the second fell silent as soon as a question came up between the participants
the first covered a wide syllabus and left the participants passive
the second moved along more slowly and stirred up exchanges
a beginner got on faster there than a seasoned practitioner
the writer advises the second arrangement in spite of its narrower syllabus
text: Dear colleague, here is the account I promised of the two courses I sat this term, since they run against each other at almost every point. The first put a large group into a tiered room: the speaker talked, we wrote, and nobody cut in. The second gathered a mere handful of us round one table, and the woman leading it fell silent the moment a question came up between us. The first covered a wide syllabus and left us diligent but idle. The second moved along at a crawl and made us talkative, muddled at times. Where the first rewarded a good page of notes, the second rewarded a mistake said out loud. A beginner got on faster there than a seasoned practitioner, because he dared say what he had not followed. If you must choose for the team, take the second, even at the cost of covering less ground.

units: a learner asks a worker in stone what learning really is
the answer takes the shape of an ordered list
the first item is consenting to dullness
the movement repeated without end is likened to water wearing away rock
the second item is accepting what is hard
an obstacle overcome leaves a mark that ease never leaves
the third item is taking account of what the material will allow
another item is bearing the harsh correction of an older hand
the last item is forgetting what has been learnt so that the hand moves before the mind
the worker in stone refuses to put a figure on the time needed
text: What is it to learn? The apprentice puts the question to the stonecutter. The answer comes as a list, its items laid out like tools along a bench. To learn, he says, is first to consent to dullness: a movement repeated without end wears its own channel, as water wears the rock it runs over. It is next to accept what is hard, not from any love of pain, but because an obstacle beaten leaves a mark that ease never presses in. It is to listen to the material, which refuses one curve and asks for another. It is to bear the eye of an older hand who corrects and offers no comfort. And it is, at the last, to forget what has been learnt, so that the hand moves before the mind does. And how many seasons does that road take? The stonecutter smiles, wipes his chisel and says such a stretch is not counted, only crossed.

units: the instructor first asks for the power to the machine to be cut
the trainee reports that the indicator light is still flashing
the instructor explains that a residual charge remains in the capacitor
that charge has to be given time to drain away
the cover is taken off by loosening the screws crosswise
uneven tightening warps the sealing gasket
the trainee then measures a residual voltage of nothing at all
the instructor requires the operation to be entered in a register before anything is put back
the procedure only holds good if every step is dated and signed
text: The instructor started by telling the trainee to cut the power to the machine and watch the indicator light go out. She reported that the light was still flashing away. He explained that a residual charge lingers in the capacitor and that they had to wait for it to drain away in full. Then he asked her to take off the cover, loosening the screws crosswise rather than one after another round the edge. She wanted to know what lay behind that rule. Uneven tightening, he said, warps the sealing gasket. She measured the residual voltage next and gave a reading of nothing at all on the dial. The instructor accepted the measurement and had her enter the operation in the register before a single part went back on. A procedure is worth nothing, he ended, unless every step is dated and signed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the growth in the number of town workshops changed the way trades were taught
families were no longer enough to supply the hands that were needed
masters took children from elsewhere into their own homes
living under one roof gave rise to written agreements
the agreements set out the length of service, the keep and the secrecy required
the ban on teaching outside the workshop protected what the trade was worth
that ban slowed the spread of technique
the guilds never settled the contradiction between secrecy and the renewal of the workforce
travelling workers carried the movements from one workshop to another
text: As workshops multiplied in the towns, the teaching of a trade changed in kind. Families could no longer supply the hands that were needed, so masters took children from elsewhere into their own homes. Living under one roof gave rise to written agreements: the length of service, the keep owed, the procedures that were not to be spoken of outside. Since secrecy protected what a trade was worth, teaching beyond the workshop door was forbidden, and that ban slowed the spread of technique. Out of it came a contradiction the guilds never settled: guarding the process meant starving the trade of fresh hands. When traffic between regions grew heavier, travelling workers carried the movements from one workshop to another all the same. Secrecy gave way through movement, then, and not by any decision of the masters.

units: material read over again feels familiar and that familiarity is mistaken for command of it
the student believes he is ready and then finds himself helpless later on
recognising a statement costs less effort than producing it from memory
the brain confuses these two sensations
the answer is to question oneself without looking at one's notes
the effort of recall fixes the memory even when it fails
the recalls have to be spread further and further apart
the spacing widens up to the point where forgetting becomes likely
the method gives an impression of failure although it works
text: Anyone studying alone runs into a known trap: material read over again feels familiar, and that familiarity passes for command of it. The reader shuts the notebook satisfied, then finds a week later that nothing will come. The mechanism is well established. Picking out a statement you have met before costs less effort than producing it from memory, and the brain confuses the two sensations. The answer lies in a reversal. Rather than read again, you put the question to yourself and hunt for the answer with your notes shut. The effort of recall fixes the trace far better than a comfortable second reading, even when it comes up empty. Those recalls are then spread out, close together at first and wider and wider afterwards, up to the point where forgetting grows likely. The method feels thankless: it gives an impression of failure while it works.

units: the narrator showed the same knot to two learners
the younger one managed it after one demonstration and two failed attempts
she asked no questions
the grown man listened closely and took notes
he questioned the narrator about the logic of the crossing
he did not manage the knot that evening
the man was trying to understand where the young one was content to copy
the narrator took his notebook away and covered his eyes
the man managed it quickly once he could not see
the narrator concludes that his explanations got in the way of the man's hands
text: I taught the same knot to two learners over the last season, and the pair of them still nag at me. The younger one needed a single demonstration: she took the rope, got it wrong twice running, then had it right without a word from me, and asked nothing at all. The other, a grown man, listened with faultless courtesy, took notes, and put sharp questions to me about why the crossing had to go that way. He did not get the knot right once, all evening. It was not that he learnt less well; he learnt differently, wanting to understand what the young one was content to copy. When I took his notebook off him at last and tied a cloth right over his eyes, his hands found the answer in three tries. The lesson I draw stings a little: my explanations had fed his head and tied up his fingers.
